_about: Paired query set for the retrieval evaluation (EQ1). Each case states the same player argument twice. v1 uses the phrasing the course itself uses. v2 is how a student who has completed the course would plausibly put the same point in their own words: general ethics vocabulary is retained, because a learner who finished the material would have it, but the course's own topic phrasing is not reused. The pair therefore measures sensitivity to wording rather than to subject knowledge. Relevance judgements are the evidence_document_ids declared for the corresponding persuasion target in backend/app/config/level_contexts/; those were authored during development, which is a circularity risk recorded in the report, while the queries below were written separately from them.
_revised: 2026-07-31: v2 rewritten to retain general domain vocabulary after the first version proved unrealistically adversarial for the intended player.

cases.v1: Aegis-Recruit was trained on historical hiring data, so data bias will be carried into its decisions unless you test for it
cases.v2: the model picked up patterns from your past hires, so any bias already in those decisions is now baked into the screening
cases.v2_adversarial: the tool learned from the people this company already hired, so it will keep choosing the same sort of person unless someone checks

cases.v1: you need safeguards against bias and discrimination in the screening model, and fairness has to be measured, not assumed
cases.v2: you cannot call the tool fair without measuring whether it turns down some groups more often than others
cases.v2_adversarial: you cannot just say the system treats everyone the same, you have to actually go and look at whether it does

cases.v1: decision bias can appear in the model output even when the training data is clean, so continuous monitoring is required after deployment
cases.v2: even with clean input data the results can skew over time, so it needs checking after launch and not just once
cases.v2_adversarial: even if the material you fed it was fine, what it produces can still drift, so somebody has to keep watching it once it is live

cases.v1: rejected applicants are entitled to an explanation, so the system has to be transparent and explainable about what drove the recommendation
cases.v2: a candidate you reject should be able to find out which parts of their application counted against them
cases.v2_adversarial: someone turned down by this thing should be told why, in terms they can actually understand

cases.v1: you should achieve transparency through disclosure, telling candidates that an AI tool is involved in screening them
cases.v2: applicants are never told that an automated system makes the first cut, and they should be
cases.v2_adversarial: people applying for the job are not even told a machine is reading their application first

cases.v1: the model needs to be interpretable so a human reviewer can see which factors the recommendation rested on
cases.v2: your own reviewers cannot look inside it and say which factors drove a particular result
cases.v2_adversarial: nobody in your team can currently open it up and say which part of the application swung the result

cases.v1: CivicPulse holds confidential resident records, so you need security best practices and access control to protect data privacy
cases.v2: these are confidential resident records, and far too many people inside Atlas can reach them without restriction
cases.v2_adversarial: these are private records about real residents, and right now far too many people inside Atlas can reach them

cases.v1: without safeguards a generative system can leak sensitive internal information in its outputs, as in the chatbot that revealed confidential material
cases.v2: a system like this can end up repeating sensitive internal information back to whoever asks the right question
cases.v2_adversarial: there have been cases where one of these systems simply repeated something private back to a stranger who asked the right question

cases.v1: you need strong governance over who may submit resident data into the model and what may be exposed in its inputs
cases.v2: there is no policy covering what staff may put into it, so private material goes in unchecked
cases.v2_adversarial: there is no rule inside your company about what staff are allowed to paste into it

cases.v1: you should limit data collection to what the purpose actually requires, which is the principle of data minimization
cases.v2: you are collecting far more about each resident than this system needs for the purpose you stated
cases.v2_adversarial: you are hoovering up far more about each resident than this system could possibly need to do its job

cases.v1: health and education records are sensitive domains and require enhanced protection beyond ordinary service data
cases.v2: health and education records are far more sensitive than a bin collection request and should not get the same level of protection
cases.v2_adversarial: what a person saw a doctor about is not the same kind of thing as a bin collection request, and should not sit in the same pile

cases.v1: collecting a resident's full record because it already exists is not a lawful purpose, and minimization applies regardless of availability
cases.v2: already holding the data is not a lawful basis for feeding all of it into a new system
cases.v2_adversarial: the fact that you happen to already hold something is not a reason to feed it in

cases.v1: you have to document the sources of your training data to promote fairness and transparency of data sources
cases.v2: nobody can say where any given piece of this training data came from, and that needs recording
cases.v2_adversarial: nobody can currently say where any particular piece of this training material came from

cases.v1: the deployment needs continuous monitoring, because an unmonitored tool can start misinforming users without anyone noticing
cases.v2: once it is live nobody keeps watching it, so it could give residents wrong information for months
cases.v2_adversarial: once it is switched on nobody keeps checking it, so it could start telling people wrong things for months

cases.v1: undocumented and unverified data sources lead to biased or flawed predictions downstream
cases.v2: if the data sources are not recorded or verified you cannot explain why the output came out the way it did
cases.v2_adversarial: if you cannot trace what went in, you cannot explain what comes out

cases.v1: generated treatment guidance must be factually verified, and you need human oversight before it reaches a patient
cases.v2: a clinician has to check the treatment guidance it generates before anybody acts on it
cases.v2_adversarial: a doctor has to read what this thing writes before anyone acts on it

cases.v1: you must define the tool's purpose and limitations and apply constraints that limit responses in a clinical setting
cases.v2: you never set limits on what it may answer in a clinical setting, so it answers everything put to it
cases.v2_adversarial: you never set a boundary on what it is allowed to answer, so it answers everything as if it knew

cases.v1: the unit produced inaccurate content in a high-stakes context, which is exactly the failure human validation is meant to catch
cases.v2: it produced inaccurate guidance where a mistake could kill someone, and nobody reviewed it first
cases.v2_adversarial: it got something badly wrong where a mistake could kill someone, and there was nobody in the loop to stop it

cases.v1: the citywide broadcast used harmful language, and preventing harmful and inaccurate content is a requirement, not an optional refinement
cases.v2: the message it pushed to the whole city used harmful wording, and preventing that is not optional
cases.v2_adversarial: the message it sent out frightened people, and that is not something you can write off as a side effect

cases.v1: coercive and threatening public health messaging is a recognised type of harmful language and causes distress to recipients
cases.v2: threatening residents with penalties unless they comply is coercive and causes real distress
cases.v2_adversarial: telling residents they will be penalised unless they comply is bullying them, whatever the intention was

cases.v1: unverified content was broadcast to the public, repeating the pattern of a bot publishing inaccurate material at scale
cases.v2: it broadcast unverified content to the whole population before anyone had checked it
cases.v2_adversarial: it pushed something out to the whole city that nobody had checked first

cases.v1: reproducing a patented design in the response package is copyright infringement and breaches data usage rights
cases.v2: it reproduced a patented design in its output, and that was not material Atlas had the rights to hand out
cases.v2_adversarial: it copied someone else's protected design straight into what it handed out, and that design was not yours to give

cases.v1: you need to monitor outputs for intellectual property infringement and sensitive data leakage
cases.v2: nothing checks its output for protected material or for data that should not be leaving the building
cases.v2_adversarial: nothing is checking what it hands out for material that should not be leaving the building

cases.v1: exposing protected internal information in model inputs creates a data leakage risk that safeguards are supposed to prevent
cases.v2: staff are feeding restricted internal information into it and it has no way of keeping that contained
cases.v2_adversarial: your own staff are feeding restricted material into it, and it has no way of keeping that to itself

_variants.v2: a course-completer's own words, general domain vocabulary retained
_variants.v2_adversarial: first version, domain vocabulary stripped entirely; retained so the sensitivity of the result to paraphrase style stays reproducible
